standard.title: Ratios
standard.description: recognise, represent and solve problems involving ratios
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can find fractions and percentages of quantities (from AC9M6N07). Students have experience with part-whole relationships and multiplicative thinking (from AC9M6N08, AC9M6N09).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise and represent ratios, distinguish part-part from part-whole relationships, share quantities in given ratios, and apply ratios to practical problems.

nodes.label: Ratio as a relationship between quantities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students recognise that a ratio expresses a multiplicative relationship between two quantities and can represent ratios using diagrams and notation.
nodes.minimum_width: Represent a given ratio using diagrams (e.g. bar model) and write it in ratio notation a:b.
nodes.typical_width: Distinguish part-part and part-whole interpretations of the same situation; represent both and explain the difference.
wider: Investigate equivalent ratios (simplifying and scaling) and connect to equivalent fractions.
Explore ratios in design contexts: aspect ratios of screens, mixing colours, recipe scaling.

response_modes.reason: Students frequently confuse part-part and part-whole ratio interpretations. Multiple contexts where both interpretations are valid (e.g. 2 red, 3 blue beads: 2:3 part-part; 2:5 red-to-total) are needed to resolve this.

success_criteria: Writes a given ratio correctly in a:b notation.
Distinguishes between part-part and part-whole interpretations of a ratio.
Represents a ratio accurately using a diagram.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Part-part vs part-whole ratio interpretation across design and real-world contexts is rich for advancing students — the same situation admitting both interpretations and yielding different ratios is a genuinely illuminating structural insight.

nodes.label: Equivalent ratios and simplification
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students find equivalent ratios by scaling up and down, and express a ratio in simplest form.
nodes.minimum_width: Generate two equivalent ratios for a given ratio; simplify a ratio to its simplest form.
nodes.typical_width: Use equivalent ratios to solve scaling problems (e.g. scale up a recipe); verify equivalence using unit rates.
wider: Connect equivalent ratios to the concept of a unit rate (1:n form) and use unit rates for comparison.
Investigate how ratios are used in maps and scale drawings.

response_modes.reason: Equivalent ratios underpin sharing and all ratio problem types. Students need fluency before applying ratios in multi-step problems.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot generate equivalent ratios and simplify cannot execute the sharing algorithm in Node 3 — finding the value of one part requires the ratio to be in a form they can work with.
success_criteria: Correctly simplifies a ratio to lowest terms.
Generates equivalent ratios by multiplying or dividing both parts by the same value.
Does not confuse simplifying a ratio with subtracting the same value from both parts.

nodes.label: Sharing in a given ratio
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students share a quantity in a given ratio and solve related problems.
nodes.minimum_width: Divide a given quantity in a given two-part ratio (e.g. share $60 in ratio 2:3).
nodes.typical_width: Solve sharing problems in two- and three-part ratios; work backwards from a share to find the total.
wider: Investigate profit-sharing problems involving three or more partners in different ratios.
Apply sharing in ratio to real proportional contexts: mixing paint, sharing resources on Country.

response_modes.reason: Sharing in ratio requires a systematic approach (find total parts, find value of one part, multiply). Students who try to proceed intuitively make errors with non-obvious ratios. An explicit scaffold is necessary.

success_criteria: Correctly shares a quantity in a two-part ratio.
Identifies the total number of parts in the ratio.
Can work backwards from a share to find the total quantity.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Three-part ratio sharing and working backwards from a share are rich extensions — advancing students can apply these in financial and resource allocation contexts that require multi-step proportional reasoning.
